stories.title: An MP without a vote, six wards that do vote, and a 09:00 bail ruling for 18 treason accused: the Thursday that Zambia's post-election politics has been waiting for
stories.excerpt: The Electoral Commission has refused to cancel the Mandevu by-election and is due on Thursday 5 November to declare the UPND's Adrian Banda MP without a ballot, while Kasonde Mwenda's bid for a High Court stay is pending. The same morning six wards in five districts vote, a three-judge High Court panel sits at 09:00 to rule on constitutional bail for Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 others, the Solwezi High Court decides where their sedition case is tried, and the President heads to Mandevu for a town hall.

image.label: Thursday 5 November
image.caption: Thursday 5 November 2026 brings a Mandevu declaration without a vote, six ward by-elections, a High Court bail ruling for 18 treason accused and a venue ruling in Solwezi.

body: Thursday 5 November was fixed by the Electoral Commission as a by-election day. It has become something else: a day on which an Electoral Commission declaration, two court rulings in two provinces and a presidential town hall all fall within a few hours of each other, and on which the questions raised by the August general election about who may stand, who may be held and where they may be tried are all, in one form or another, up for decision.

body.text: Mandevu: a declaration, not a poll

body: News Diggers reported on Wednesday 4 November that the Electoral Commission of Zambia has rejected calls to cancel the Mandevu parliamentary by-election. Three candidates withdrew: the Leadership Movement's Ntazana Musukuma, the independent Daniel Daka and the Forum for Democracy and Development's Daniel Chisenga. That left the UPND's Adrian Banda as the only validly nominated candidate for the poll scheduled for Thursday. The Commission's position, given by its Chief Electoral Officer Brown Kasaro in reply to a press query on Monday 2 November, is that the Constitution allows the sole remaining candidate to be declared elected. The Tonse Alliance's secretary general, Muhabi Lungu, had asked for the election to be cancelled, describing the sudden withdrawal of the opposition candidates as undemocratic.

Zambia Monitor reported on Friday 30 October that the Commission's notice said Mr Banda would be declared duly elected without the need for an election, that the three withdrawal letters were dated Wednesday 28 October, and that the notice gave no reasons for the withdrawals and did not say whether the Commission had received formal complaints about the threats and intimidation that some opposition figures had alleged during the campaign.

The declaration is contested in court. Zambia Monitor reported on Tuesday 3 November that Kasonde Mwenda, the president of the Economic Freedom Fighters, has filed an ex-parte application in the Lusaka High Court for leave to seek judicial review of the Commission's decision of 28 August to abandon the original Mandevu parliamentary process and order a fresh election, together with the notices and directions that followed it. The application, stamped on Monday 2 November under cause number 2026/HTR/1316 and brought under Order 53 of the Rules of the Supreme Court, names the Commission and the Attorney-General as respondents and asks for a stay of the 5 November election until the legal questions are decided.

body.text: There is no legal provision or authority empowering the Commission to take the action it has taken.
body.attribution: Kasonde Mwenda, president of the Economic Freedom Fighters, in the application reported by Zambia Monitor on Tuesday 3 November

body: The Zambian Observer reported on Wednesday that President Hakainde Hichilema is scheduled to hold a community town hall in Mandevu on Thursday, at the Mutambe Community Grounds, with residents of Mandevu, Marrapodi, Matero, Matero East and Justine Kabwe Ward expected to attend and questions on fuel prices, inflation, empowerment loans and local services anticipated. The Observer's report quoted the President telling residents, "We are coming to you." That account has not been confirmed by a second outlet.

Voting does take place on Thursday, but only in local government wards. News Diggers reported on Sunday 1 November that Commissioner Zevyanji Sinkala said six wards in five districts will go to the polls, with training of poll staff held on Saturday 31 October in Lwingishi Ward in Mansa. The Commission had originally set 5 November for two parliamentary by-elections, in Mandevu and Lumezi North, eleven ward by-elections and the Mbala mayoral election. The UPND is unopposed in Mandevu, Lumezi North and the Mbala mayoral race after rivals withdrew, and was the only validly nominated candidate in five wards, named in the report as Maako, Siluwe, Upangoma, Mulimambango and Simanvwa.

At 09:00 on Thursday a three-judge panel of the Lusaka High Court is due to deal with the constitutional bail application of 18 people held on treason and terrorism-related allegations, among them the opposition leader Brian Mundubile, his running mate Makebi Zulu and Harry Finblay. Zambia Monitor reported on Thursday 29 October that the panel of Judges Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga had granted the State a further adjournment after the Attorney-General, Mulilo Kabesha, said the applicants' reply to the State's affidavit in opposition was bulky and needed study, but warned that it was the final adjournment: if a party is not ready on Thursday the court will close the matter and rule on the documents and arguments already filed. The 18 were brought from Mukobeko Maximum Security Correctional Facility, and the report said the public and the media were restricted from photographing them.

For the applicants, Milner Katolo opposed what he called a fourth adjournment, argued that the National Prosecutions Authority's own manual recognises constitutional bail where trial proceedings have been delayed, and raised concerns about Mr Finblay's health, saying he had missed appointments with a cardiologist in South Africa. Dates for the substantive petition are to be set after the bail ruling.

body.text: The court has insisted and emphasised that this is the last adjournment.
body.attribution: Milner Katolo, counsel for the applicants, at the Lusaka High Court, as reported by Zambia Monitor on Thursday 29 October

body: The Solwezi High Court is due the same day to rule on whether the separate sedition case against Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu stays in Solwezi or moves to Lusaka, News Diggers reported on Wednesday. That ruling, and a press-freedom complaint about the treatment of journalists covering it, are reported in the Courts section of this edition.

body.title: Thursday and Friday at a glance
items: **Mandevu** — the ECZ is due to declare Adrian Banda MP without a vote; Kasonde Mwenda's application for a stay (2026/HTR/1316) is before the Lusaka High Court
**Six wards** in five districts vote; the UPND is already unopposed in five others, in Lumezi North and for Mbala mayor
**09:00, Lusaka High Court** — three judges on constitutional bail for Mundubile, Zulu and 16 others
**Solwezi High Court** — ruling on where the Mundubile and Zulu sedition case will be heard
**Mandevu, Mutambe Community Grounds** — presidential town hall, the Zambian Observer reports
**Friday 6 November** — Situmbeko Musokotwane presents the 2027 budget to the National Assembly

body.confirmed: The ECZ has said it will not cancel the Mandevu by-election and that the sole remaining candidate can be declared elected (News Diggers, Zambia Monitor). Mwenda's judicial review application and its request for a stay are on the High Court file under 2026/HTR/1316 (Zambia Monitor). Six wards vote on 5 November (News Diggers). The treason bail matter is set for 09:00 on 5 November before Judges Mulenga, Chibwili and Wishimanga, with no further adjournment allowed (Zambia Monitor). Cabinet has approved the 2027 budget for presentation on Friday (Times of Zambia, News Diggers).
body.unverified: Whether the High Court will hear or grant Mwenda's stay before the declaration is made; whether the bail panel will rule on Thursday or hear further argument first; the outcome of either ruling. The allegations of threats and intimidation behind the Mandevu withdrawals have been reported but not established. The presidential town hall in Mandevu rests on a single outlet's report.

stories.title: Cleared for Friday: Cabinet approves the 2027 budget and a UAE trade pact, as Musokotwane rules out a third supplementary budget and tells the FRA to fund itself from maize sales
stories.excerpt: Cabinet has approved the proposed 2027 National Budget, which Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane presents to the National Assembly on Friday 6 November, and has also cleared Zambia to sign a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement with the United Arab Emirates. In Parliament on Tuesday the minister said the 2026 spending on maize was a deliberate hedge against a forecast 2027 drought, ruled out a third supplementary budget and said the five new ministries would be absorbed without extra recruitment.

image.label: Friday's budget
image.caption: Cabinet approved the 2027 National Budget at its third meeting of the second term; Situmbeko Musokotwane presents it to the National Assembly on Friday 6 November 2026.

body: The 2027 budget has cleared Cabinet and goes to the National Assembly on Friday 6 November. The Times of Zambia and News Diggers both reported on Wednesday 4 November that the Chief Government Spokesperson, Elvis Nkandu, announced the approval in a statement on Tuesday, after what the Times described as the third Cabinet meeting of President Hakainde Hichilema's second term, chaired at State House on Friday 30 October.

According to News Diggers, the statement said Cabinet had found the country on a positive economic trajectory, that sustained macroeconomic stability is critical to the Grow Zambia Agenda, and that ministers had called for prudent fiscal management in 2027. Neither outlet's report carried budget figures; those come on Friday. The Times added that Cabinet also approved Zambia's signature of a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement with the United Arab Emirates, together with an implementation, import-surveillance and periodic review mechanism for the agreement.

The Finance and National Planning Minister, Situmbeko Musokotwane, gave MPs a preview of the budget's logic on Tuesday 3 November, News Diggers reported, during the adoption of the Budget Committee's report on the amended 2026 Annual Borrowing Plan. He said the government is spending in 2026 to reduce the cost of food security in 2027, because a drought is forecast for next year, and that the 2027 budget will give the Food Reserve Agency little from the Treasury since the agency's maize sales should pay for its next purchases.

body.text: There will not be a third request for a supplementary budget.
body.attribution: Situmbeko Musokotwane, Minister of Finance and National Planning, in the National Assembly on Tuesday 3 November, as reported by News Diggers

body: He also said, according to the same report, that the cost of the five new ministries could be absorbed without additional recruitment, that concessional borrowing is prioritised as the cheapest option but that such sources are limited, and that external borrowing carries foreign exchange risk.

body.text: The K19.9 billion behind the remarks

body: The second supplementary budget of 2026, presented on Thursday 22 October, explains why the minister is talking about maize. Zambia Monitor reported that the Supplementary Estimates of Expenditure No. 2 total K19.9 billion, of which K15.8 billion, or 79 per cent, goes to agriculture: K14.7 billion to pay farmers who supplied maize to the Food Reserve Agency, which bought 2.7 million tonnes this year against a target of 500,000 tonnes, and K1.1 billion for the Farmer Input Support Programme. Smaller items were K1.3 billion for the Ministry of Finance, including K1 billion in Asycuda processing fees remitted to the Zambia Revenue Authority, K540 million for the Higher Education Loans and Scholarship Board, K422.5 million for defence and a K300 million contingency vote. The financing was listed as K18 billion in domestic borrowing, K1.3 billion in additional revenue, K510.8 million in donor funds and smaller savings.

body.title: The numbers so far
items: **K19.9 billion** — second supplementary budget of 2026, presented 22 October
**K14.7 billion** — of that, arrears to farmers who sold maize to the FRA
**2.7 million tonnes** — FRA purchases in 2026, against a 500,000-tonne target
**K18 billion** — of the supplementary financed by domestic borrowing
**Friday 6 November** — 2027 budget presented to the National Assembly

body: The budget arrives in the week Moody's moved Zambia's rating from Caa2 to Caa1, a step that economists quoted by News Diggers on Wednesday read as a sign of creditor confidence while noting the rating remains in speculative territory, and the Cabinet statement's language about stability and prudence will be read against that. What the figures on Friday have to reconcile is a farm sector owed billions, a drought the government says it is already paying to pre-empt, and a stated preference for borrowing only where it is cheapest.

stories.title: Foreign cash in, copper, gold and gemstones out: the FIC says a K1 billion smuggling syndicate ran for three years and gold-linked terrorist financing is 'on our doorsteps'
stories.excerpt: The Financial Intelligence Centre says it has uncovered a mineral smuggling syndicate worth about K1 billion that operated between 2022 and 2024, bringing foreign currency into Zambia to buy illegally mined copper, gold and gemstones and taking them out untaxed. Director General Clement Kapalu told a gold supply chain workshop in Lusaka that unregulated gold rushes such as Mufumbwe's breed illicit markets and that the country's money laundering risk has moved from medium to high.

image.label: K1 billion in minerals
image.caption: The Financial Intelligence Centre described a K1 billion mineral smuggling syndicate that operated between 2022 and 2024 at a gold supply chain workshop in Lusaka.

body: The Financial Intelligence Centre has put a figure on the illicit mineral trade it says it has traced. The Centre's Director General, Clement Kapalu, told a workshop in Lusaka on gold supply chain practices, held from an anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing perspective, that the FIC has uncovered a mineral smuggling syndicate worth about K1 billion that operated between 2022 and 2024, News Diggers reported on Wednesday 4 November.

The mechanics, as he described them, ran in both directions. Foreign cash was smuggled into Zambia and used to buy copper, gold and gemstones that had been mined illegally; the minerals were then taken out of the country without the taxes due on them. The Zambian Observer, which reported the workshop on Tuesday 3 November, said the minerals were exported outside established customs procedures and that the syndicate also involved foreign currency allegedly brought into Zambia through illicit mineral dealings. Its report noted that it remains unclear who was behind the transactions and how the minerals left the country without customs clearance.

Mr Kapalu singled out unregulated gold rushes, giving the example of Mufumbwe, as the kind of event that gives rise to illicit markets, according to News Diggers. The Observer reported that he said Zambia's money laundering risk rating has moved from medium to high, and that he raised concern about suspected links between illegal gold mining and the financing of extremist groups in the region.

body.text: The link between gold and terrorist financing is not a distant problem, it's on our doorsteps.
body.attribution: Clement Kapalu, Director General of the Financial Intelligence Centre, at a gold supply chain workshop in Lusaka, as reported by News Diggers on Wednesday 4 November

body: The Observer's report placed the remarks alongside calls from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and the World Gold Council for tighter controls on mineral trading, including systems that trace gold from the mine to the point of sale. It also framed the FIC's concern as going beyond lost revenue to the growing role of criminal networks in the mineral trade, especially gold.

body.title: What the FIC said
items: **About K1 billion** — value of the syndicate's dealings, 2022 to 2024
**Copper, gold and gemstones** — bought with smuggled foreign cash from illegal miners
**Exported untaxed** — outside customs procedures, by means not yet explained
**Medium to high** — Zambia's money laundering risk rating, according to Kapalu
**Mufumbwe** — the gold rush cited as an example of an unregulated market

body: No individuals or companies were named in either report, and neither said whether the findings have been passed to investigators or what, if anything, has followed. The figure lands in a week when the Treasury has been emphasising fiscal discipline ahead of Friday's budget.

stories.title: 'Partners and competitors': ZESCO tells the Zim-Zam summit in Livingstone the market is opening to private producers, as ZESA counts 635 megawatts under construction
stories.excerpt: The third Zimbabwe-Zambia Energy Projects Summit opened in Livingstone this week, with ZESCO's chief operating officer saying the utility now sees independent power producers as both partners and competitors, and ZESA's group chief executive arguing that strong, well-paid utilities are what attract investors. The three-day meeting at the Radisson Blu Mosi-oa-Tunya, hosted by Copperbelt Energy Corporation, runs to Thursday 5 November.

image.label: Zim-Zam 2026
image.caption: The third Zimbabwe-Zambia Energy Projects Summit runs from 3 to 5 November 2026 at the Radisson Blu Mosi-oa-Tunya in Livingstone.

body: The third edition of Zim-Zam, the Zimbabwe-Zambia Energy Projects Summit, opened in Livingstone this week with government officials, investors, the two national utilities and private developers in the room, and with the familiar question of how declared project pipelines become financed plants. The Zambian Observer, carrying an ICU TV report, said on Wednesday 4 November that the opening session was dominated by calls for stronger partnerships and more foreign direct investment.

ZESCO's Chief Operating Officer, FitzPatrick Kapepe, told the summit that Zambia has made progress in opening its electricity market to private participation, and that the utility now regards independent power producers as both partners and competitors, according to the report. His Zimbabwean counterpart, ZESA Holdings Group Chief Executive Cletus Nyachowe, argued that strong, well-structured utilities are what bring investment, and that better regulation and reliable payment systems are the foundation of investor confidence.

body.text: For a public sector project to take off, you need a strong utility.
body.attribution: Cletus Nyachowe, Group Chief Executive of ZESA Holdings, at the Zim-Zam summit in Livingstone, as reported by ICU TV and carried by the Zambian Observer

body: Jason De Carteret, Chief Executive of Solarcentury Africa, put the developer's view: what makes deals work, he said, is the existence of the customer. The report carried no new investment figures or capacity commitments from the opening day.

The organiser, EnergyNet, set out the agenda in a release published in October and carried by Pan African Visions. The summit runs from Tuesday 3 to Thursday 5 November at the Radisson Blu Mosi-oa-Tunya under the theme of how the two countries have unlocked foreign direct investment through connectivity, credibility and cooperation. Copperbelt Energy Corporation is the country host; the release notes that CEC financed the second phase of its Itimpi project through a green bond on the local capital market. ZESA Holdings, it says, reports 635 megawatts of private generation under construction in Zimbabwe and a further 730 megawatts moving towards financial close.

Projects named as informing the discussions include the Lumwana Super Pit and Kansanshi S3 expansions, Chisamba Solar and the Kariba floating solar scheme, with sessions on generation for mining and industry, transmission and interconnectors and the Southern African Power Pool. Zimbabwe's Minister of Energy and Power Development, July Moyo, and Zambia's Minister of Green Economy and Environment, Gilbert Siame, are listed among the speakers, alongside the permanent secretaries Mulele Mulele and Arnold Simwamba and the Industrial Development Corporation's chief executive, Cornwell Muleya. Petrodex is the summit sponsor, with Bowmans and Standard Bank as lead sponsors.

body.title: Zim-Zam 2026
items: **3–5 November** — Radisson Blu Mosi-oa-Tunya, Livingstone; third edition since 2024
**Country host** — Copperbelt Energy Corporation
**635 MW** — private generation ZESA reports under construction in Zimbabwe; 730 MW heading to financial close
**Projects in view** — Lumwana Super Pit, Kansanshi S3, Chisamba Solar, Kariba floating solar

body: EnergyNet's own framing was that the opportunity is clear and the priority is now delivery. The test of this edition is whether the regulatory and payment reforms the utilities described on Wednesday are enough to move the next round of projects from pipeline to construction.

stories.title: 'Observers play a critical role': Hichilema receives the EU mission and pledges reforms, as its chief observer says lethal force in the Mundubile raid feeds public anxiety
stories.excerpt: President Hakainde Hichilema has met the EU Election Observation Mission led by Michael McNamara, thanked it for its recommendations and said his administration remains committed to reforms that deepen democracy, according to reports carried by the Zambian Observer. The meeting followed the mission's final report and its chief observer's remarks on a raid linked to Brian Mundubile, the closure of courts in August and the Electoral Commission's unpublished results, which the government has contested.

image.label: The President and the mission
image.caption: President Hichilema met the EU Election Observation Mission led by Chief Observer Michael McNamara after the mission published its final report on the 13 August 2026 elections.

body: The day after the European Union's observers published their final verdict on the August election, the President received them. The Zambian Observer reported on Wednesday 4 November that President Hakainde Hichilema met a delegation from the EU Election Observation Mission led by its Chief Observer, Michael McNamara, thanked the mission for its observations and recommendations and for its congratulations on his re-election, and said his administration would continue to pursue reforms that strengthen democratic institutions and deepen cooperation with the EU. A TV Yatu report carried by the same outlet put the meeting on Tuesday 3 November.

body.text: Election observers play a critical role in strengthening and deepening our democracy.
body.attribution: President Hakainde Hichilema, on meeting the EU Election Observation Mission, as reported by the Zambian Observer on Wednesday 4 November

body: The President was also reported as saying that a flourishing democracy is key to the Grow Zambia Agenda. The tone was warmer than the government's written reply to the report, in which the Chief Government Spokesperson, Elvis Nkandu, argued that observers do not have access to the intelligence, security and law enforcement information available to the State.

body.text: What the mission said this week

body: News Diggers reported on Wednesday that, at the presentation of the final report, Mr McNamara spoke of shrinking democratic space and growing signs of government control after the 13 August election, and cited the mission's media monitoring finding that ZNBC gave the President up to 96 per cent of its political airtime. The government questioned the findings, the report said, on the ground that the EU lacked access to security and law enforcement information.

The TV Yatu report carried by the Zambian Observer set out further points from the mission: concern at the lack of information about a raid on a private residence linked to the opposition leader Brian Mundubile and at the alleged use of lethal force in that operation, which the mission described as a source of public anxiety; a finding that the physical closure of access to the courts between 24 and 26 August curtailed access to justice and electoral due process; and concern that the Electoral Commission of Zambia has not published the results of the 13 August election. The same report said Mr Nkandu had challenged parts of the report as not reflecting the country's security situation, and had said some political actors and their supporters had been under investigation for some time over serious alleged criminal conduct.

body.title: Established and disputed
items: **Established** — the mission's final report was published on 3 November; the President met the mission and pledged reforms (Zambian Observer, two reports)

**The mission's findings** — ZNBC airtime of up to 96 per cent for the President, court closures of 24–26 August, unpublished results and the Mundubile raid (News Diggers, TV Yatu via the Zambian Observer)
**The government's reply** — that observers lack access to security information and that investigations predate the report (News Diggers, Zambian Observer)

body: The meeting does not change the report's status: its recommendations have no legal force and are addressed to a government that has already said it disputes some of the findings. What it does signal is that the presidency wants to be seen engaging with the mission rather than only rebutting it. Whether that engagement extends to the mission's specific recommendations is a question for the parliamentary session now under way, which turns to the budget on Friday.

stories.title: Solwezi or Lusaka: the High Court rules on Thursday where Mundubile and Zulu answer sedition charges over two Facebook posts, as a press group protests at reporters' treatment
stories.excerpt: The Solwezi High Court is due on Thursday 5 November to decide whether the sedition case against Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu stays in North-Western Province or moves to Lusaka, where the defence says the alleged offences, two Facebook posts of 14 August about vote counting, were committed. The Free Press Initiative has condemned what it calls the harassment and obstruction of journalists covering the proceedings by police and correctional officers.

image.label: Solwezi or Lusaka
image.caption: The Solwezi High Court rules on 5 November 2026 on whether the sedition case against Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu is heard in Solwezi or transferred to Lusaka.

body: Of the two courtrooms Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu are due before on Thursday, the one in Solwezi decides the smaller question, but it is the one that has produced a month of argument. News Diggers reported on Wednesday 4 November that the Solwezi High Court is scheduled to rule on Thursday 5 November on whether the seditious practices case against the NRPUP presidential candidate and his running mate should remain in Solwezi or be transferred to Lusaka.

The defence wants Lusaka. Its argument, as reported, is that the alleged offences were committed there and that both men were in the capital at the time. The case concerns Facebook posts of Friday 14 August, the day after the general election, about the counting of votes. Mr Mundubile is alleged to have posted that the NRPUP was leading according to its parallel vote tabulation and to have called on the Electoral Commission of Zambia to resume counting after it was suspended. Mr Zulu, according to an earlier account in the Zambian Observer that drew on News Diggers' reporting, is alleged to have posted that Mr Mundubile would address the nation and to have urged the public to stand by.

The venue fight began in the Solwezi Magistrate's Court. The Zambian Observer reported on Tuesday 6 October that the two men challenged that court's jurisdiction and asked for the case to be heard in Lusaka, arguing that witnesses would be easier to reach there, with supporters gathering outside the court when they appeared. The transfer question is now before the High Court in Solwezi.

The two men are also among the 18 applicants whose constitutional bail application on separate treason and terrorism-related allegations is before a three-judge panel of the Lusaka High Court at 09:00 the same morning. Zambia Monitor reported that the Lusaka panel chose 5 November as the only available date in part because the first and second applicants had another matter listed for Tuesday 3 November.

The Daily Nation reported on Wednesday that the Zambia Free Press Initiative has condemned the reported harassment and obstruction of journalists covering the Solwezi High Court proceedings. Its founder, Joan Chirwa, described the alleged conduct of police and correctional service officers as unacceptable and warned that intimidation of journalists undermines press freedom. The Daily Nation's report carried no response from the police or the Correctional Service.

body.confirmed: The Solwezi High Court has set Thursday 5 November for its ruling on the venue application (News Diggers). The charges concern Facebook posts of 14 August 2026 about the counting of votes (News Diggers, Zambian Observer). The Free Press Initiative has publicly complained about the treatment of journalists at the Solwezi court (Daily Nation).
body.unverified: The sedition allegations themselves, which both men contest and which no court has yet tried; the FPI's account of harassment, on which the police and Correctional Service have not been reported as responding; and the outcome of Thursday's ruling.

stories.title: Not guilty, says the Lima MP: Kelvin Kaunda denies assaulting a man during the August campaign, the State lists five witnesses, and trial may open on 17 November
stories.excerpt: Kelvin Kaunda, the NRPUP Member of Parliament for Lima, has pleaded not guilty before Lusaka magistrate Mutinta Mwenya to one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm over an incident on 7 August 2026 in which police allege Anthony Mwamba, 26, was struck with stones and fists on Zingalume Road. The prosecution says it will call five witnesses; the case returns on Tuesday 17 November and Mr Kaunda remains on the K30,000 bail granted by the High Court last week.

image.label: The Lima MP's plea
image.caption: Kelvin Kaunda, MP for Lima, pleaded not guilty to assault occasioning actual bodily harm before a Lusaka magistrate, the Zambian Observer reported on 4 November 2026; the case returns on 17 November.

body: Three weeks after his arrest and a week after his release on bail, the Member of Parliament for Lima has entered his plea. The Zambian Observer reported on Wednesday 4 November that Kelvin Kaunda pleaded not guilty in Lusaka, before Magistrate Mutinta Mwenya, to one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm contrary to section 248 of the Penal Code, confirming that he understood the charge. The State said it would rely on five witnesses, and the court adjourned the matter to Tuesday 17 November, when the trial may begin. Mr Kaunda remains on bail.

The particulars, as reported by the Observer, are that on Friday 7 August 2026, in Lusaka District, Mr Kaunda assaulted Anthony Mwamba and caused him actual bodily harm. Zambia Monitor reported the police account at the time of the arrest: a statement by the police spokesperson, Chipo Kaitisha, on Friday 16 October said Mr Mwamba, 26, of Soweto Compound, had reported on 7 August that he was assaulted at about 19:30 that evening on Zingalume Road during campaign roadshows, suffering a deep cut to the forehead and a swollen upper lip. The police said it was alleged that stones and fists were used.

Mr Kaunda was detained from Thursday 15 October, first at Lubwa Police Post and then at Mwembeshi Prison, News Diggers reported. The Lusaka High Court's Judge Kaumbi Ndulo granted him K30,000 cash bail with two working sureties in the same sum, and he was released on Tuesday 27 October after meeting the conditions. In an interview reported by News Diggers on Thursday 29 October, he described his detention as a political baptism, said he had not been discouraged, accused the criminal justice system of treating citizens differently according to their political affiliation and said he had forgiven those who, in his words, had falsely accused him. The same report described Mr Mwamba as a suspected UPND member.

body.title: The case so far
items: **7 August 2026** — alleged assault on Zingalume Road during campaign roadshows; complaint lodged the same day
**15–16 October** — Kaunda detained; police announce the charge under section 248 of the Penal Code
**27 October** — released on K30,000 High Court bail with two sureties
**This week** — pleads not guilty before Magistrate Mutinta Mwenya; State names five witnesses (reported 4 November)
**17 November** — case returns; trial may begin

body.confirmed: Kaunda has pleaded not guilty to one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and is on bail pending a hearing on 17 November (Zambian Observer). The complaint, the complainant's reported injuries and the charge were set out in a police statement of 16 October (Zambia Monitor). Bail of K30,000 was granted by Judge Kaumbi Ndulo (News Diggers).
body.unverified: Whether the assault took place as alleged: that is the question for trial, and Mr Kaunda denies it. The complainant's political affiliation, described by News Diggers as suspected rather than established.

body: The case is one in which the conduct of August's campaign is being tested in court after the fact. The defence has given no indication yet of the case it will run; the first of the State's five witnesses is expected on 17 November if the trial opens as scheduled.

stories.title: Thirty for Burundi: Lwandamina recalls Chanka Zimba from Portugal, keeps Daka and Sakala and brings in Zesco's Kennedy Musonda for the qualifiers on 13 and 17 November
stories.excerpt: Interim coach George Lwandamina has named a 30-man provisional Chipolopolo squad for the two 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Burundi, at the Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola on Friday 13 November and in Bujumbura on Tuesday 17 November. The list recalls striker Chanka Zimba, now at Vitória de Sernache in Portugal, alongside Patson Daka, Fashion Sakala and Lameck Banda, and rewards Zesco United's Kennedy Musonda and Red Arrows' Zephaniah Phiri and Ackim Mumba. It will be cut to 26.

image.label: Thirty for Burundi
image.caption: George Lwandamina named a 30-man provisional Zambia squad on 4 November 2026 for the AFCON 2027 qualifiers against Burundi on 13 and 17 November.

body: The provisional list for the Burundi double-header is out, and it is a blend of the familiar and the recalled. ZamFoot reported on Wednesday 4 November that the interim coach George Lwandamina has named 30 players for the back-to-back Group I qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations: Zambia host Burundi at the Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola on Friday 13 November and travel to Bujumbura for the return on Tuesday 17 November.

The headline inclusion is Chanka Zimba, the striker who has just joined GD Vitória de Sernache in Portugal and returns to the national set-up. He is one of five forwards, with Patson Daka, Fashion Sakala, Albert Kangwanda and Zesco United's Kennedy Musonda, whose domestic form earns him a place. Red Arrows supply the defender Zephaniah Phiri and the midfielder Ackim Mumba, two of the local players ZamFoot singled out.

body.title: Provisional squad, as reported by ZamFoot
items: **Goalkeepers (4)** — Willard Mwanza, Lawrence Mulenga, Luka Mainza, Victor Chabu
**Defenders (10)** — Mathews Banda, Zephaniah Phiri, Owen Mwamba, David Hamansenya, Gift Mphande, Tinklar Sinkala, Ricky Chanda, Jackson Phiri, Dominic Chanda, William Kamwanga
**Midfielders (11)** — Lameck Banda, Gamphani Lungu, Joshua Mutale, Wilson Chisala, Owen Tembo, Obino Chisala, Miguel Chaiwa, Joseph Liteta, Ackim Mumba, Kelvin Mwanza, Allan Mumba
**Forwards (5)** — Fashion Sakala, Albert Kangwanda, Patson Daka, Kennedy Musonda, Chanka Zimba

body: The squad assembles in Ndola on Thursday 5 November with its locally based players; those abroad are expected when the FIFA window opens on Monday 9 November. Mr Lwandamina is expected to trim the group to 26 before the first match. Some players on the list are also with the under-23 side, which plays Burkina Faso in Ouagadougou on Wednesday 11 November and at the National Heroes Stadium four days later, so the final selection will depend on how the two coaches share them.

ZamFoot's report puts Zambia second in Group I with three points from two matches, one behind the leaders Algeria, with Togo also on three and Burundi bottom on one. Two wins over Burundi would put Zambia in a strong position with two rounds to play; anything less leaves the group open. The finals, branded AFCON Pamoja 2027, are co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania from 19 June to 17 July 2027.

The 30 names are a provisional selection and will change: the test for the interim coach is whether the six players he cuts, and the eleven he starts in Ndola, show a settled idea of how this team wants to play after a transitional year.

sources.title: Lwandamina names 30-man provisional squad for Zambia's Burundi double-header

stories.title: Two Copper Queens on the shortlists: Barbra Banda is up for CAF Women's Player of the Year again and Hazel Nali for Goalkeeper of the Year, decided in Lagos on 7 December
stories.excerpt: CAF has published its 2026 awards shortlists and two Zambians are on them: Orlando Pride's Barbra Banda, the 2024 winner, among ten nominees for Women's Player of the Year, and goalkeeper Hazel Nali among ten for Women's Goalkeeper of the Year. Zambia is not on the Women's National Team of the Year shortlist. The ceremony is at the Wole Soyinka Centre in Lagos on Monday 7 December.

image.label: Banda and Nali
image.caption: Barbra Banda and Hazel Nali were named on CAF's 2026 awards shortlists on 3 November 2026; the ceremony is in Lagos on 7 December.

body: Barbra Banda is back on the shortlist she topped two years ago. The Confederation of African Football published its 2026 awards nominations on Tuesday 3 November, and the Copper Queens captain, who plays for Orlando Pride in the United States, is one of ten players in contention for Women's Player of the Year. She won the award in 2024, becoming the first Zambian to do so, as ZamFoot noted in its report of the nominations.

She is joined on CAF's lists by the goalkeeper Hazel Nali, named among ten nominees for Women's Goalkeeper of the Year. CAF's published list gives her club as ZESCO. No other Zambian appears in the women's categories released so far, and Zambia is not among the ten teams shortlisted for Women's National Team of the Year.

The Player of the Year field, as published by CAF, is Marine Dafeur of Algeria, Marie Ngah Manga, Michaely Bihina and Monique Ngock of Cameroon, Portia Boakye of Ghana, the Malawian sisters Tabitha and Temwa Chawinga, Hanan Ait El Haj of Morocco, Thembi Kgatlana of South Africa and Banda. Bihina, a Benfica goalkeeper, is also on the goalkeepers' list, where Nali's rivals include Chloe N'Gazi of Algeria, Cynthia Konlan of Ghana, Mercy Sikelo of Malawi, Fatoumata Karantao of Mali, Khadija El-Rmichi of Morocco, Christiana Uzoma of Nigeria, Adji Ndiaye of Senegal and Kaylin Swart of South Africa.

body.title: CAF Awards 2026
items: **Women's Player of the Year** — Barbra Banda (Zambia, Orlando Pride) among ten nominees
**Women's Goalkeeper of the Year** — Hazel Nali (Zambia, ZESCO) among ten nominees
**National Team of the Year** — Zambia not shortlisted; Algeria, Cabo Verde, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Malawi, Mali, Morocco, Nigeria and South Africa are
**Still to come** — Interclub Player, Coach and Club of the Year, after the CAF Women's Champions League in Egypt
**Monday 7 December** — ceremony at the Wole Soyinka Centre, Lagos

body: CAF said the nominations reflect achievements in international and club football over the year, and that performances at the CAF Women's Champions League in Egypt will be weighed before the three club-related shortlists are finalised. It did not set out the voting procedure in its announcement.

For Zambian women's football the two names carry different stories. Banda's nomination follows her 2024 award, the first for a Zambian; Nali's is recognition for a goalkeeper in a sport whose attention usually goes to the forwards. Whether either collects a trophy in Lagos will be decided over the next month; the absence of the Copper Queens from the team shortlist is a reminder of a year in which the individual stars outshone the collective results.

analysis.title: Declared, not elected: what Thursday settles in Mandevu and what it leaves open
analysis.body: By Thursday evening Mandevu should have a Member of Parliament who received no votes, and the arguments about how that happened will not be over. The Electoral Commission's position is narrow and procedural: three candidates withdrew, one remains, and the Constitution provides for the one to be declared. The objections run on two tracks that should be kept apart. The first, from the Tonse Alliance, is political: that the withdrawals were not free, and that a declaration built on them rewards whoever applied the pressure. The Commission has not said whether it received complaints. That dispute is about facts nobody has yet established. The second track, Kasonde Mwenda's, is legal and goes back further: whether the Commission had any power on 28 August to abandon the original Mandevu process and order a fresh one, or whether that was a question only the High Court could decide. If a judge grants leave, the declaration could be made and later unmade; if not, the case ends quietly. What to watch is the order of events on Thursday: a stay granted before the declaration changes everything, one considered afterwards changes very little in practice.

analysis.title: Two benches, one morning: why the bail ruling matters more than the venue ruling
analysis.body: Thursday puts Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu before two courts at once, and the two decisions are not of equal weight. The Solwezi question, whether a sedition case over two Facebook posts is tried in North-Western Province or in Lusaka, is about convenience, witnesses and, the defence would say, the optics of trying a Lusaka matter in another province. Whatever the answer, a trial follows somewhere. The Lusaka question is about liberty. Eighteen people have been held at Mukobeko on treason and terrorism-related allegations while the State has not yet set a date for the substantive case, and the three-judge panel has already said it will not adjourn again. Constitutional bail is not a verdict on guilt; it is a finding about whether continued detention before trial is justified. The State's case is that the allegations are grave and its preparation thorough; the applicants' is that delay itself is the injustice and that the prosecution's own manual says so. What to watch is less the headline outcome than the reasoning, and whether the panel rules on the papers or hears argument first. Either way, a date for the petition itself comes next.

analysis.title: Reading Friday's budget: the maize bill, the borrowing plan and the rating
analysis.body: The 2027 budget arrives with its framing already written. Cabinet has used the words stability and prudence; Moody's has moved the rating from Caa2 to Caa1; and the Finance Minister has told MPs there will be no third supplementary budget this year. The harder reading is in what the supplementary estimates reveal. Of K19.9 billion in extra 2026 spending, K14.7 billion is owed to farmers who sold 2.7 million tonnes of maize to a Food Reserve Agency that planned to buy 500,000, and K18 billion of the financing is domestic borrowing. The minister calls this spending ahead of time against a forecast drought, and says the agency must now fund its purchases from maize sales rather than the Treasury. The strongest case for that approach is that a full granary in a dry year is worth more than the interest; the strongest case against is that domestic borrowing on that scale crowds out credit and that an agency funded by its own sales has every incentive to sell dear in a lean season. Friday's numbers to watch are the FRA line, the domestic financing figure and whether the five new ministries really cost nothing extra.
